title: Broke

jokes.text: It's 4:30 in the morning. Do you know where your kids are? If you are Ryan's parents or Pam's parents or my parents, you do. They're gonna be in this van. With me. Who am I? Nothing to fear. I am just a 44-year-old guy with a paper route.
jokes.setup: Michael opens with a dramatic, ominous monologue reminiscent of a late-night PSA — 'Do you know where your kids are?' building dread about who is with them
jokes.punchline: The grand reveal is that he is just a middle-aged man doing early-morning paper deliveries, framed as a heroic adventure
jokes.explanation: This is an exceptional cold open. The PSA parody structure is perfectly executed — Michael inadvertently sounds like a predator ('nothing to fear... they're gonna be in this van with me') before deflating into 'a 44-year-old guy with a paper route.' The self-awareness of the joke is entirely accidental from Michael's perspective, which is peak Michael Scott comedy. The character integration is near-perfect: only Michael would narrate his paper delivery route like a gritty thriller. Scores 8+ because the setup/subversion ratio is excellent and it lands as a genuine comedic concept, not just a quirky line.

jokes.text: Time to make the donuts!
jokes.setup: Michael is enthusiastically doing early-morning deliveries and calls out this catchphrase
jokes.punchline: He's delivering paper, not donuts — the phrase is wildly inapplicable and delivered with maximum sincerity
jokes.explanation: Functional joke — Michael repurposing a Dunkin' Donuts ad slogan for his paper delivery is classically Michael, but the laugh relies heavily on the audience's familiarity with that ad and Michael's enthusiasm rather than any novel comedic construction. Works as a character beat more than a crafted joke.

jokes.text: Come on. No, I promise I won't do it again. Come on. De-nied!
jokes.setup: Michael is apparently trying to do something (likely a silly gesture or bit) that Ryan has rejected before
jokes.punchline: The childlike pleading followed by Ryan's emphatic 'De-nied!' suggests Michael keeps attempting some annoying physical bit during deliveries and Ryan has developed a whole rejection ritual
jokes.explanation: The joke lives in the implication — we can't see what Michael is doing, but Ryan's emphatic 'De-nied!' and the fact that Michael promised not to do it again suggests a recurring annoyance. The dynamic of Ryan having developed systems to manage Michael's behavior is very funny in its own right. Moderately effective without the visual.

jokes.text: Ever since I've gotten clean, there's something about fresh morning air... that just really makes me sick.
jokes.setup: Ryan begins a confessional in the style of someone who has turned their life around — 'ever since I've gotten clean' suggests redemption and newfound appreciation for simple things
jokes.punchline: The expected inspirational beat ('makes me feel alive') is subverted by '...that just really makes me sick' — Ryan hates this and is only here out of necessity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The misdirection is elegant: 'ever since I've gotten clean' primes an uplifting sentiment, then the pause before '...that just really makes me sick' lands perfectly. It's also deeply character-specific — Ryan's recovery is treated as background detail while his primary complaint is that mornings are unpleasant. Maximum economy, character-perfect. Scores high because the structure is genuinely skilled and could be a highlight reel moment.

jokes.text: Time to make the donuts! (second instance)
jokes.setup: Michael repeats his delivery catchphrase for the second time in the cold open
jokes.punchline: The repetition itself becomes the joke — Michael genuinely thinks this is his thing now
jokes.explanation: The repetition is intentional and works as a running gag beat, but it's diminishing returns on an already middling joke. Scores lower than the first instance because callbacks need to add something and this doesn't escalate or subvert.

jokes.text: Boner patrol! Arrest that man! Your donuts make me go nuts!
jokes.setup: Michael is doing his energetic early-morning delivery routine
jokes.punchline: He shouts increasingly unhinged phrases at no one in particular at 5 AM — 'Boner patrol! Arrest that man!' is completely inexplicable and delivered with pure enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: 'Boner patrol' is the kind of thing Michael would unironically shout at 5 AM and find hilarious. 'Your donuts make me go nuts' is an accidental dirty rhyme that Michael probably thinks is completely wholesome. The absurdist escalation of his morning energy is very Michael, though the joke lacks a clean structure — it's more of a character impression than a constructed joke.

jokes.text: We got the van at a used car lot. We think it says 'Alleluia Church of Scranton' in Korean. It was either this or an old school bus with an owl living in it.
jokes.setup: Pam gives a matter-of-fact talking-head about the company's transportation situation
jokes.punchline: The casual acceptance that their van may advertise a Korean church, and that the alternative was literally a school bus with an owl — delivered without any distress
jokes.explanation: Solidly written — the specificity of 'Alleluia Church of Scranton in Korean' is funnier than a generic foreign-language van, and 'an old school bus with an owl living in it' is perfectly absurd. Pam's deadpan delivery makes it work — she's not complaining, just reporting facts. The two-option joke structure (bad option A vs. worse option B) is well-executed.

jokes.text: You didn't happen to bring any coffee, did you, Michael? — Milk and sugar. — Awesome. You're a life saver. — Wait, is this just milk and sugar? — That's what I said. — Do you drink this every day? — Every morning.
jokes.setup: Ryan hopefully asks Michael if he brought coffee; Michael says 'milk and sugar'
jokes.punchline: It IS just milk and sugar — no coffee. Michael drinks this concoction every morning as if it were a normal beverage and sees no issue with this
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. Michael offering 'milk and sugar' sounds like he's describing coffee components, so the reveal that there IS no coffee — and that he's been drinking pure milk and sugar every morning as a lifestyle choice — is both absurd and completely in character. Ryan's dawning horror ('Do you drink this every day?' / 'Every morning.') is the perfect straight-man reaction. High character integration: only Michael would do this.

jokes.text: We have 20... Excuse me. Sorry. Sorry, no. It's... It's a paper company now. It's not for the church.
jokes.setup: The MSPC van (marked as an Alleluia Church of Scranton in Korean) pulls up to a delivery location
jokes.punchline: A confused recipient apparently thinks they're receiving a church delivery — Michael or the crew has to clarify that this is a paper company, not a religious institution, while the van screams otherwise
jokes.explanation: A payoff for the van setup — the confusion is earned and the moment is funny in context. The callback works but doesn't escalate beyond what was already established in the van joke. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I'd just like to point out that I have been here less time than these guys. — Why are you telling me this? — I just think the bar should be lower for a newbie. — Is this something you really want to have said? — I don't want to have said that. But I think it's important that you know it.
jokes.setup: David Wallace is dressing down the Dunder Mifflin Scranton team for losing clients to MSPC; Charles interjects to preemptively excuse himself
jokes.punchline: Charles argues, in real-time, for a lower performance bar because he's new — then when challenged, admits he shouldn't have said it but doubles down because 'it's important that you know it'
jokes.explanation: Superb character joke. Charles has been positioned as a hard-nosed authority figure, so watching him make a completely cowardly, self-serving argument — then KNOW it was wrong but insist on having made it anyway — is a perfect subversion. 'I don't want to have said that. But I think it's important that you know it' is excellent writing: it's the logic of someone who can't back down. The Office rarely gets such clean irony out of Charles. High scores across the board.

jokes.text: I got your memo. Thank you. I'm putting my foot down when it comes to expense reports. Waste not, want not. — Well said, Angela.
jokes.setup: David Wallace has written a memo asking for cost-saving ideas in a corporate crisis; Angela responds by announcing she's cracking down on expense reports
jokes.punchline: In the middle of a company-wide crisis losing major clients, Angela's response is to police petty expense reports — and Wallace thanks her sincerely with 'Well said, Angela'
jokes.explanation: Classic Angela — her response to a macro business crisis is a micro bureaucratic crackdown, which is perfectly in character. Wallace saying 'Well said, Angela' with evident sincerity when she's contributed nothing of value adds a nice layer of organizational dysfunction. Solid character joke, not exceptional.

jokes.text: Been there, done that.
jokes.setup: Angela announces she's cracking down on expense reports; the camera presumably catches Meredith's reaction
jokes.punchline: Meredith dismisses the entire expense report situation with a bored 'Been there, done that' — implying she has a history of being caught on expense reports and has moved past caring
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfectly Meredith. The joke is in the implication — she's been disciplined for expense reports before and is completely unfazed. Economy is near-perfect. Loses points for being a fairly minor beat.

jokes.text: You know what we need? We need some couches. — We should really consider getting a delivery guy. — You know what you would love? It's if we built a loft. — Why would I love that? — Can we afford a delivery guy? — Like in a dorm room. You put your desk underneath, you have your loft up top. You can sleep up top. — I know what a loft is. — Most dorm rooms don't even have that. — Most do in the magazines.
jokes.setup: The MSPC team is trying to figure out how to improve their tiny office operation; practical suggestions (delivery guy) are interspersed with Michael's completely impractical ones (couches, loft)
jokes.punchline: Michael insists on explaining what a loft is to Pam (who knows), Ryan argues 'most dorm rooms have lofts... in the magazines,' and the conversation derails entirely from the actual business problem
jokes.explanation: 'Most do in the magazines' is the highlight — Ryan's insistence on a detail he clearly doesn't actually know is very Ryan. Michael explaining what a loft is to someone who already knows is classically condescending-Michael. The whole sequence captures how this 'company' operates: three people talking past each other while a real problem goes unaddressed. Moderately funny throughout with a couple of standout lines.

jokes.text: Stanley, pay attention.
jokes.setup: David Wallace is about to address the entire office in a serious meeting about the business crisis
jokes.punchline: Before he even begins, he has to specifically call out Stanley — implying Stanley is already visibly checked out during the CEO's address
jokes.explanation: Three words and maximum character economy. Stanley's complete indifference to corporate authority — to the point where even a visiting CEO has to personally address him — is a running character truth about Stanley. Very efficiently delivered.

jokes.text: Maybe, and I don't know, if you had just returned Michael's call, none of us would've lost clients. — I've been wondering that myself lately.
jokes.setup: David Wallace is reassuring the staff about the MSPC situation; Jim interjects with a pointed observation about how this whole disaster could have been prevented
jokes.punchline: Wallace responds not with defensiveness but with 'I've been wondering that myself lately' — an unusually candid admission that undercuts his authority and makes Jim's boldness land even better
jokes.explanation: A good moment — Jim's willingness to point out the elephant in the room to his boss's boss is classic Jim, and Wallace's disarmingly honest response ('I've been wondering that myself') is funnier than a defensive reaction would have been. The joke is partly in the subversion of expected corporate defensiveness.

jokes.text: Come along, afterthought.
jokes.setup: Charles adds Jim to the conference room meeting as an afterthought after initially wanting only Dwight; Dwight addresses Jim as they walk in
jokes.punchline: Dwight's gleeful 'Come along, afterthought' perfectly captures his joy at being preferred over Jim while being too smug to hide it
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — two words that capture the entire Dwight-Jim dynamic in this episode perfectly. Dwight is reveling in his moment of superiority and can't resist rubbing it in, which is completely in character. The word choice 'afterthought' is specific and funny (not 'loser' or 'second-pick'). High quotability because it's so reusable in everyday contexts. One of the episode's tightest jokes.

jokes.text: A lame attempt at humor. Swing and a miss.
jokes.setup: Pam offers a weak joke about their pricing ('Corporate greed?') in response to the accountant pointing out their prices are unsustainably low
jokes.punchline: Ryan immediately and mercilessly critiques the joke with sports metaphors, as if he's a professional joke evaluator
jokes.explanation: Ryan calling out Pam's weak joke with 'A lame attempt at humor. Swing and a miss.' is very Ryan — he fancies himself a superior wit. The meta quality of one character critiquing another character's joke is a nice layer, and the double-sports-metaphor is efficiently done. Character-specific enough to score above average.

jokes.text: Right. So... Why don't you explain what that is... So they can under... — Explain what that is. — Explain what you think that is. — Just explain.
jokes.setup: The accountant explains variable cost pricing; Michael is clearly confused and tries to reassert himself by asking the accountant to explain it — implying Michael will then explain it to the others
jokes.punchline: Michael can't even finish the sentence — Pam and Ryan interrupt him progressively, simplifying to 'Just explain.' — because they all know Michael doesn't understand it either
jokes.explanation: A nicely constructed cringe moment — Michael's instinct to perform authority ('Why don't you explain what that is so they can under—') collapses in real time as his team cuts him off because they see through it. The progressive interruption ending in 'just explain' shows Pam and Ryan's quiet exasperation. Good character integration for all three.

jokes.text: Hold on, hold on. Ty, I would like you to crunch those numbers again. — It's a program. There's no such... — Just crunch 'em, please. — Crunch. Did it help?
jokes.setup: Ty (the accountant) has presented damning financial projections showing MSPC is doomed; Michael refuses to accept this and asks Ty to 'crunch the numbers again'
jokes.punchline: Ty explains that it's a computer program — there is no re-crunching — but Michael insists. Ty presumably presses a key and says 'Crunch. Did it help?' with total deadpan. The numbers have not changed.
jokes.explanation: A wonderful small moment. Michael's magical thinking about 'crunching numbers' — as if re-running the math will produce a better answer — is a universal comic concept executed perfectly here. Ty's deadpan 'Crunch. Did it help?' is excellent: he's gone along with the absurdity while making it clear nothing changed. High quotability, highly rewatchable. Among the episode's best small jokes.

jokes.text: Hi, Jerry. Michael Scott. This is slightly embarrassing. I'm going to have to ask you to pay me a little bit more money for that delivery we dropped off yesterday. We did. We got the check. But we're just going to need a much, much bigger check.
jokes.setup: Michael is calling clients after learning MSPC is underpricing itself, asking them to retroactively pay more
jokes.punchline: 'We got the check. But we're just going to need a much, much bigger check.' — Michael is literally calling clients to ask them to voluntarily give him more money after already paying
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of Michael's solution to the pricing crisis — calling clients and asking for bigger checks — is very funny and very Michael. 'We got the check. But we're just going to need a much, much bigger check' has great rhythm. Character-specific because only Michael would think this was a viable business strategy.

jokes.text: When a child gets behind the wheel of a car and runs into a tree, you don't blame the child. He didn't know any better. You blame the 30-year-old woman who got in the passenger seat and said, 'Drive, kid. I trust you.'
jokes.setup: Michael is calling a client and apparently explaining why the prices are going up, using an elaborate metaphor
jokes.punchline: The 'child' is Michael; the '30-year-old woman' who told the child to drive is apparently... the client? The metaphor collapses into absurdity — Michael is blaming his customer for trusting him too much
jokes.explanation: This is Michael Scott at his most Michael Scott. The metaphor sounds like it will be self-deprecating ('don't blame the child... he didn't know better') but becomes an accusation against his own client — YOU are responsible for trusting me. The specificity of '30-year-old woman' in the passenger seat is wonderfully absurd. It scores 8+ because the comedic logic is both internally consistent and perfectly character-revealing: Michael genuinely cannot conceive of taking responsibility, so his metaphor inadvertently blames the victim. High character integration.

jokes.text: I say we fill Michael's office with bees. My apiarist owes me a favor. — Really? Does he do good work or... — No, Jim. I use a bad apiarist.
jokes.setup: The Dunder Mifflin team is brainstorming solutions to the MSPC problem; Dwight suggests filling Michael's office with bees
jokes.punchline: Jim's understated 'Does he do good work or...' treats this as a completely normal conversation, and Dwight's exasperated 'No, Jim. I use a bad apiarist' is the perfect non-answer — addressing Jim's question while ignoring the insanity of the situation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and among The Office's great small moments. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) Dwight has an apiarist, which is funny; (2) Dwight's apiarist owes him a favor, which implies a whole bizarre relationship; (3) Jim completely ignores the 'fill office with bees' part to ask about quality of work; (4) Dwight's deadpan 'No, Jim. I use a bad apiarist' is the perfect response — insulted by the implication, defending his apiarist, while still in the insane premise. Maximum economy, perfect character voices for both Jim and Dwight. Approaches 8+ anchor standard — comparable to 'Never go with a hippie to a second location' in wit and economy.

jokes.text: I say we fill Michael's office with bees. My apiarist owes me a favor.
jokes.setup: Charles and David Wallace are discussing how to handle the Michael Scott Paper Company problem in a serious business meeting
jokes.punchline: Dwight's solution is to fill Michael's office with bees, delivered as a legitimate proposal, and the fact that he has a personal apiarist who owes him favors
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Multiple layers working simultaneously: (1) Dwight's escalation to bees as a corporate solution, (2) the absurd specificity that he has an apiarist (beekeeping is perfectly Dwight-coded), (3) that the apiarist owes him a favor (implying a whole off-screen relationship), and (4) the casual confidence with which he floats this in a boardroom. The joke grows funnier the more you think about it. 'My apiarist owes me a favor' may be the most Dwight sentence ever written. Earns 8.5+ on craft.

jokes.text: I saw you called. — You're just out of business? — We have maybe a month. — I don't know what I'm gonna do. — Don't worry about it. We'll figure it out. We'll be okay. — That's what Michael said. — Only this time we will be okay.
jokes.setup: Jim sneaks out to call Pam; she reveals the Michael Scott Paper Company is nearly broke
jokes.punchline: Pam says 'That's what Michael said' with obvious skepticism; Jim's response — 'Only this time we will be okay' — is both reassuring and a perfect gentle dig at Michael
jokes.explanation: A warm joke that also lands comedically — the acknowledgment that Michael says everything is okay and it never is, paired with Jim's gentle distinction between Michael's reassurance and his own, is sweet and funny. Character-specific to Jim's relationship with both Pam and Michael.

jokes.text: Idiot. Idiot. Idiot. — My new 'Dwight' ring. — I like it. — Good, right? — Idiot, we're starting back up. This is Dwight, by the way.
jokes.setup: Jim has set his ringtone to Dwight saying 'Idiot' — presumably a recording — so he knows when Dwight is calling
jokes.punchline: The phone rings 'Idiot. Idiot. Idiot.' and Jim cheerfully explains it's his Dwight ringtone; the call itself is Dwight calling him an idiot to tell him the meeting is restarting
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed layered joke. Jim has set Dwight's ringtone to Dwight calling him an idiot, which: (1) shows Jim's commitment to pranking Dwight even in this context, (2) the callback that the call IS Dwight calling him an idiot to come back to the meeting means the ringtone is literally accurate, and (3) Dwight helpfully identifies himself at the end. The concentric layers (ringtone joke → the actual call is the joke) are very well constructed. High character integration: this is quintessential Jim.

jokes.text: Did I ever tell you about the day that Steve Martin died? — Steve Martin's not dead. — I know. But I always thought that the day that he died would be the worst day of my life. And I was wrong. It's this.
jokes.setup: Michael appears to be sharing a profound personal story about loss
jokes.punchline: Steve Martin is not dead — Michael is using a hypothetical pre-grieved death to frame his current situation as worse than even the death of his comedy hero. The joke is both absurd and genuinely pathetic in the best way.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a strong contender for the series. The construction is exceptional: Michael opens with a solemn 'did I ever tell you about the day Steve Martin died?' — the straight correction ('Steve Martin's not dead') — 'I know' — and then the reveal that Michael has pre-grieved Steve Martin's death and assigned it as his personal worst-case scenario, only to discover that THIS is actually worse. The joke accomplishes three things simultaneously: it's absurd (pre-grieving Steve Martin), it's deeply in character (Michael's hero is a comedian; his emotional life is theatrical), and it's unexpectedly poignant. The rhythm is perfect. Scores 8.7 — exceptional craft, one of the episode's true standouts. Comparable to the vasectomy anchor for character-perfect emotional-comedy blending.

jokes.text: So Jim and I are getting married and the wedding's really expensive, so I tried to get a job on the weekends to earn extra money. I applied to Old Navy, Target and Walmart. None of 'em called me back. Not even for an interview.
jokes.setup: Pam reveals in a talking head that she applied for weekend retail jobs to help pay for the wedding
jokes.punchline: None of them called her back — not even for an interview. Pam, a professional office worker, was rejected by retail giants without even getting a courtesy callback
jokes.explanation: A great cringe joke played with complete sincerity. Pam's embarrassment and bewilderment at being rejected by Old Navy — delivered without any self-awareness about what that implies — is very funny. 'Not even for an interview' is the escalating beat that sells it. The pause implied between the two sentences is key. Character-specific: Pam would genuinely find this humiliating and report it to camera without realizing how it sounds.

jokes.text: I never went to Thailand. — Really? — I went to Fort Lauderdale. — Was it nice? — Yeah, it was amazing. There was a great pad thai place, though. — I love pad thai. — You never had pad thai.
jokes.setup: Ryan admits he never actually went to Thailand (something he'd previously claimed), having instead gone to Fort Lauderdale
jokes.punchline: Ryan salvages his Thailand claim by noting there was 'a great pad thai place' in Fort Lauderdale, then tells Pam she's never actually had pad thai — an odd flex from someone who went to Fort Lauderdale and called it Thailand
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ryan character joke. Ryan lying about going to Thailand and then doubling down to correct Pam about pad thai — while he himself went to Fort Lauderdale — is perfectly Ryan: performative, slightly mean, and completely lacking self-awareness. 'There's a lot I haven't done' from Pam is the bonus beat. The joke captures Ryan's essential nature in about 60 words.

jokes.text: There's a lot I haven't done.
jokes.setup: Pam has just learned she's never had pad thai (per Ryan) and reflects
jokes.punchline: Pam's resigned 'There's a lot I haven't done' — referencing her limited world experience while working at a failing paper company in a van — is both self-deprecating and genuinely melancholy
jokes.explanation: A quieter beat that works as a coda to the Ryan/pad thai joke. Maximum economy — five words that suggest Pam's entire sense of her unlived life. Works better in context than as a standalone.

jokes.text: There is a hive of bees outside the front door. We kidnap the queen, extract her alarm pheromones, place them on a flushable wipe, put that in his bathroom.
jokes.setup: David Wallace has noted there are bees outside; Dwight immediately sees this as tactical opportunity and presents a detailed plan
jokes.punchline: Dwight's bee plan is both insanely specific (alarm pheromones, flushable wipe) and completely disproportionate to the business problem — he has clearly thought about this for a long time
jokes.explanation: A callback that escalates the original bee joke beautifully. The specificity of the alarm pheromone plan — especially the 'flushable wipe' detail — shows Dwight has genuinely thought this through. 'Flushable wipe' is the golden word choice: mundane, hygienic, and specific in a way that's both funnier and more disturbing than just 'cloth.' High character integration: Dwight's militaristic thinking applied to a business dispute via beekeeping knowledge is quintessentially Dwight.

jokes.text: I can't believe I'm about to say this, but... the cheapest option... is to make Michael an offer.
jokes.setup: After brainstorming (including bee attacks), David Wallace arrives at the logical conclusion that buying Michael out is cheapest
jokes.punchline: 'I can't believe I'm about to say this' — Wallace's disbelief at his own corporate logic is the joke. Michael has won, and the CFO of Dunder Mifflin can barely say it.
jokes.explanation: A solid plot-comedy moment — the humor is in Wallace's reluctant admission. The line itself is more of a pivot than a crafted joke, but the reaction it implies (the audience understands Michael has actually won) gives it comedic weight.

jokes.text: But you didn't. Oh, man!
jokes.setup: Wallace says 'Yes, I was gonna say the same thing — we should buy him out'; Jim immediately notes Wallace did NOT say it first
jokes.punchline: 'But you didn't. Oh, man!' — Jim catches Wallace trying to take credit for the idea with a gleeful, slightly childlike response
jokes.explanation: Jim calling out a CFO for trying to take credit for an idea he didn't say — with 'But you didn't. Oh, man!' — is very Jim: he can't help himself even in a high-stakes meeting. The 'Oh, man!' is the right level of theatrical disappointment. Good character beat.

jokes.text: If only Michael had children. That's how you really apply the pressure. — What is wrong with you?
jokes.setup: The team is discussing how to pressure Michael into accepting a deal
jokes.punchline: Dwight suggests leveraging Michael's children — except Michael has no children — as a pressure tactic; Jim's 'What is wrong with you?' is the straight-man response to Dwight's complete willingness to use children as negotiating leverage
jokes.explanation: Dwight's casual suggestion to leverage nonexistent children as pressure — stated with complete seriousness — is a good dark-comedy beat. Jim's 'What is wrong with you?' is the audience surrogate. The joke is slightly undercut by the fact that Michael doesn't have children, making it a moot point that Dwight doesn't even register.

jokes.text: We're not hiring. — Actually here for something else. — I can't make you laugh right now.
jokes.setup: Jim arrives at MSPC to discuss the buyout; Michael greets him with two pre-emptive deflections
jokes.punchline: 'I can't make you laugh right now' — Michael assumes Jim's primary interest in visiting is to be entertained by Michael, and this is how he declines
jokes.explanation: 'I can't make you laugh right now' is a quietly brilliant line — Michael declining to be funny as if it's a service he provides on demand, and as if his funny-ness is Jim's primary reason for visiting. It captures Michael's self-image (entertainer first, businessman second) while being completely character-specific. Very efficient.

jokes.text: Are you being serious? — He's bluffing. — What you don't understand is that this company's worthl... — We don't have... — I'm here to learn as little information as possible.
jokes.setup: Jim tells Michael that Dunder Mifflin wants to buy them out; Michael reacts with genuine excitement while Ryan and Pam nearly blow the negotiation by revealing they're broke
jokes.punchline: Jim cuts off Ryan mid-sentence ('this company's worthless') and Pam mid-sentence ('we don't have...') with 'I'm here to learn as little information as possible' — Jim is doing damage control in real time
jokes.explanation: Excellent ensemble cringe comedy. The escalating series of interruptions — Ryan trying to confess they're worthless, Pam trying to confess they have nothing — while Jim desperately shuts them down with 'I'm here to learn as little information as possible' is beautifully constructed. Jim's line is both funny as a meta-negotiation tactic and as a description of good poker-face strategy. High marks across the board.

jokes.text: Maybe. — Three yes.
jokes.setup: Jim asks if MSPC would be receptive to a buyout; Michael, Pam, and Ryan all say 'maybe' — trying to play it cool
jokes.punchline: Jim immediately translates: 'Three yes.' — stripping away their negotiating pretense entirely
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — 'Three yes.' is two words that perfectly puncture their thin negotiating facade. Jim sees through them immediately and says so flatly. The speed of the translation is the joke. Very quotable.

jokes.text: We're not only tight-ends, we are also quarterbacks. — Missed the last part. — That's a pun. — Got it.
jokes.setup: Michael attempts a sports metaphor/pun as Jim leaves; Jim says he missed the last part
jokes.punchline: Ryan clarifies 'That's a pun' as if that explains everything; Jim says 'Got it' — accepting that Michael made a pun without having understood it or needing to
jokes.explanation: The joke within the joke is that the pun itself isn't very good (tight-ends/quarterbacks as a metaphor for being both defensive and offensive in negotiations), so nobody really needs to understand it. Ryan explaining 'that's a pun' with complete earnestness and Jim accepting this as sufficient information is the real joke. Functional.

jokes.text: OK, so you're not going to reveal in any way that we're broke. Of course not. That we're having any problems at all. Just to reiterate, none of us is going to say anything that might indicate we are going broke. There is no way in hell that I'm going to say that we're broke. — I'm really worried I'm gonna say it.
jokes.setup: Michael is coaching the team before the negotiation meeting — telling them repeatedly not to say they're broke
jokes.punchline: Michael repeats the word 'broke' four times in his instructions not to say broke, ending with Pam's 'I'm really worried I'm gonna say it' — which is the most self-aware and honest moment in the scene
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed escalation joke. Michael's pre-negotiation pep talk consists almost entirely of saying 'broke' — the very word he's warning them not to say — four times in a row, each time with slight variation ('going broke,' 'that we're broke,' etc.). Pam's closing 'I'm really worried I'm gonna say it' is the perfect button: it acknowledges both the obvious failure of Michael's coaching and her own anxiety. This is a genuine craft achievement — the structure (repeating the forbidden word) is funny AND the coda lands the punchline. Scores 8.0 legitimately.

jokes.text: How the turntables...
jokes.setup: Michael arrives at Dunder Mifflin — his old workplace — to negotiate as a rival company CEO; he wants to deliver a triumphant line
jokes.punchline: 'How the turntables...' — Michael's attempt at 'how the tables have turned' collapses mid-phrase, leaving the malapropism hanging
jokes.explanation: One of The Office's most iconic Michael Scott lines. 'How the turntables...' is a perfect malapropism: Michael attempts a triumphant idiom ('how the tables have turned'), scrambles it into 'how the turntables,' and then trails off — either because he lost confidence mid-sentence or because he thinks that's actually the phrase. The genius is that it's unclear which. The trailing ellipsis makes it worse/better: he doesn't even finish the corrupted phrase. Maximum economy (four words). It has entered the broader cultural vocabulary and is one of the most quoted Office lines ever. Scores 8.5 craft (not 9+ because the construction is accidental/simple) but 9.0 impact and 10.0 quotability — it has clearly become a cultural touchstone.

jokes.text: In order to expedite these negotiations, we are prepared to make you a very generous offer. — And we are prepared to reject that offer. — You haven't even heard... — Never accept their first offer. — What is your second offer? — $12,000.
jokes.setup: Wallace opens negotiations with a 'very generous offer'; Michael and Ryan immediately reject it before hearing it, following negotiation advice they've clearly prepared
jokes.punchline: Ryan's 'What is your second offer?' jumps straight to demanding offer #2 — and the 'second offer' of $12,000 is both insultingly low AND the escalated version of their first offer
jokes.explanation: Good negotiation comedy — Michael and Ryan have clearly rehearsed 'never accept the first offer' and deployed it robotically, skipping straight to demanding the second offer. The $12,000 reveal as the 'generous' second offer is well-timed. The joke works because of how mechanically they apply half-remembered negotiation advice.

jokes.text: I'll see your situation and I'll raise you a situation. Your company is losing clients left and right. You have a stockholder meeting coming up and you're going to have to explain why your most profitable branch is bleeding. So they may be looking for a little change in the CFO. I don't need to wait out Dunder Mifflin. I think I just have to wait out you.
jokes.setup: Wallace has laid out why MSPC is vulnerable (small, new, losing money); Michael appears outgunned
jokes.punchline: Michael's rebuttal is genuinely competent corporate counter-pressure — 'I'll see your situation and raise you a situation' — and he correctly identifies Wallace's personal vulnerability. The joke is that Michael is accidentally good at this.
jokes.explanation: 'I'll see your situation and raise you a situation' is a great Michael line — poker metaphor applied wrongly but landing correctly. More importantly, Michael's actual argument is sound, which subverts all expectations. The comedy comes from Michael accidentally being right through bluster. High character integration because this is Michael's core comedic contradiction: incompetent in the ways we expect, competent in the ways we don't.

jokes.text: $60,000? — We are so... — rich. — Jerry, the one that got away.
jokes.setup: Wallace has offered $60,000 buyout; the MSPC team retreats to discuss privately and reacts with euphoria
jokes.punchline: Pam starts 'We are so...' — implying she's about to say 'screwed' or 'broke' given their actual state — but Michael finishes 'rich.' Michael then pivots to lamenting a client ('Jerry, the one that got away') in the middle of this celebration
jokes.explanation: Good moment — the inversion of the 'broke' callback ('we are so... rich'), plus Michael immediately personalizing business as romance ('Jerry, the one that got away') is very character-specific. Pam's pause before 'rich' does a lot of work suggesting what she was about to say.

jokes.text: May I ask why you're leaving the Michael Scott Paper Company? — Really? — Please hold.
jokes.setup: In the middle of the buyout celebration, Pam answers the phone — apparently a client calling to leave MSPC
jokes.punchline: The client's answer to 'why are you leaving' is apparently so obvious that they just say 'Really?' before putting them on hold — the company is so visibly failing that the reason needs no explanation
jokes.explanation: A nice timing joke — negotiating a buyout while simultaneously losing clients captures the MSPC's chaotic state. 'Really?' as a response to 'why are you leaving' implies the reason is self-evident (they're clearly failing). Good economy, good timing.

jokes.text: May I have your attention? The Michael Scott Paper Company is broke. — What? How'd you hear that? — They've been calling their clients and begging them to pay more money. They're desperate. — Which can only mean one thing. They're total failures.
jokes.setup: Charles has apparently done some detective work and discovered MSPC is broke, which he announces to Wallace with great excitement
jokes.punchline: Charles concludes this discovery with 'Which can only mean one thing. They're total failures.' — his triumphant conclusion right as MSPC is in the process of extracting a $60,000 buyout from him
jokes.explanation: Charles's triumphant revelation of information that comes too late to matter is an irony-forward joke. His dramatic 'Which can only mean one thing. They're total failures.' — while Wallace is upstairs offering them $60,000 — is dramatic irony executed well. Charles's self-satisfaction makes the joke land.

jokes.text: Great work. I mean, great detective work. 'Cause this must be the first case you've ever cracked. — You don't crack a case. That has a pejorative connotation. Like calling a policeman a cop. You solve a case, and yes, I've solved plenty.
jokes.setup: Jim sarcastically praises Dwight's 'detective work' for discovering MSPC is broke
jokes.punchline: Dwight corrects Jim on the proper terminology — 'you don't crack a case, you SOLVE a case' — treating this semantic distinction as deeply important while Jim's sarcasm sails completely over him
jokes.explanation: Classic Jim/Dwight dynamic — Jim's sarcasm completely bypassed by Dwight who latches onto a semantic technicality. The cop/policeman analogy is a nice specific touch. The joke is well-constructed but familiar territory for this pairing.

jokes.text: What are your top five cases? — I'm gonna answer Charles. — Because you've solved zero cases. — One. Case of the beet bandit. Missing beets from all over the farm. No footprints. Inside job. Mose in socks. Case closed.
jokes.setup: Jim asks Dwight to list his top five cases; Dwight tries to redirect to Charles's question
jokes.punchline: 'Case of the beet bandit. Missing beets from all over the farm. No footprints. Inside job. Mose in socks. Case closed.' — Dwight has investigated beet theft on his own farm and solved it by finding Mose wore socks to avoid leaving footprints
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Case of the beet bandit' is already funny (beets, Dwight's farm, Dwight as detective). The solution — 'Mose in socks' — is the perfect escalation: the culprit is Dwight's live-in cousin, who was stealing beets from their shared farm, and the forensic clue was the absence of footprints (socks). The specificity of 'inside job' applied to a family beet-theft is wonderful. 'Case closed' delivered with complete seriousness is the button. This scores 8.5 because the comedic world-building in five words ('Mose in socks') is exceptional craft — it implies an entire universe of Dwight/Mose farm crimes.

jokes.text: Do not go anywhere near the conference room. — Done. — Because you have embarrassed me for the last time today. — Got it? — I'm not following you. — You two are morons. — Got it. — Get out.
jokes.setup: Charles attempts to dismiss Dwight and Jim from their bickering in front of Wallace
jokes.punchline: Dwight and Jim both cheerfully follow Charles's commands ('Done,' 'Got it') while clearly not understanding or caring about his embarrassment; Charles's mounting fury ('You two are morons') gets met with 'Got it.'
jokes.explanation: Solid sequence — Dwight and Jim's combined inability to pick up social cues unites them briefly. 'You two are morons. — Got it. — Get out.' is a good closing beat. The joke is well-executed but not the episode's strongest.

jokes.text: How could you do this to me? You just cost me $60,000. — Why would you get the whole thing? It's a lot of money. — But we need money coming in every week. We need jobs. — Wouldn't you rather have a fishing pole than a fish? — I would rather have $60,000, honestly.
jokes.setup: Michael has apparently interrupted the negotiation — either nearly revealing they're broke or insisting on jobs instead of just cash; Ryan is furious
jokes.punchline: Michael defends himself with the 'fishing pole vs. fish' proverb; Ryan immediately and honestly rejects the metaphor: 'I would rather have $60,000, honestly.'
jokes.explanation: 'I would rather have $60,000, honestly' is a perfectly Ryan response — cutting through Michael's folk wisdom with blunt self-interest. The addition of 'honestly' is the right word: it's not an argument, it's just Ryan's preference stated plainly. Good character joke.

jokes.text: I want my old job back. I want my old parking space back. I want a Sebring. — They don't make them anymore.
jokes.setup: Michael is listing his demands for the buyout — jobs, parking spaces — escalating to wanting a new Chrysler Sebring
jokes.punchline: Wallace notes that Chrysler discontinued the Sebring — Michael's demand is literally impossible to fulfill, and it's that specific car
jokes.explanation: Michael demanding a Sebring is perfect — it's a mid-range, slightly tacky convertible that is quintessentially Michael Scott aspirational. Wallace deflating the demand with 'They don't make them anymore' is the ideal response. The specificity of the car brand (not 'a convertible' but a Sebring specifically) is what elevates this above a generic joke.

jokes.text: And I want Charles gone. — I am not firing Charles. He's very valuable. — That's very kind of you to say. — I need him gone.
jokes.setup: Michael demands Charles be fired; David refuses and compliments Charles; Charles thanks David
jokes.punchline: Charles saying 'That's very kind of you to say' — responding to a compliment while being in the room where someone is actively demanding his termination
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe comedy of situation. Charles's polite 'That's very kind of you to say' in response to a defense of his job while the attacker sits across the table is wonderfully awkward. The social absurdity of the moment — Charles has to respond to a compliment in an incredibly hostile context — is mined well.

jokes.text: I need him gone. — Then I want Pam back. — You already have a new receptionist. — Sales. — Pam's not a salesperson. — Yes, she is. At the Michael Scott Paper Company, in its heyday. — That's right.
jokes.setup: Michael is insisting on Charles being fired; Wallace refuses; Michael pivots to demanding Pam back
jokes.punchline: 'At the Michael Scott Paper Company, in its heyday.' — MSPC has existed for weeks and is currently broke; Michael referring to its 'heyday' is both absurd and touching. Pam's 'That's right' confirms it.
jokes.explanation: 'At the Michael Scott Paper Company, in its heyday' is a great line — the MSPC is four weeks old and currently bankrupt, and Michael refers to it as having a heyday. Pam's earnest 'That's right' doubles down on the absurdity. The joke works both as comedy and as an inadvertent love letter to their little failed company. High character integration: Michael's grandiosity applied to his own three-person operation is perfect.

jokes.text: You know, David? I don't care if Ryan murdered his entire family. He is like a son to me.
jokes.setup: Wallace is resisting rehiring Ryan due to his history of costing Dunder Mifflin hundreds of thousands of dollars
jokes.punchline: Michael's defense of Ryan — 'I don't care if Ryan murdered his entire family. He is like a son to me.' — equates mass family murder with Ryan's financial crimes as equally forgivable offenses
jokes.explanation: A very strong line. The structure is perfect: acknowledge the hypothetical worst crime possible ('murdered his entire family'), dismiss it entirely, then provide the justification ('he is like a son to me'). The joke captures Michael's unconditional, child-like loyalty to Ryan — who has repeatedly betrayed and looked down on him — in a way that's both funny and genuinely revealing of character. The 'like a son to me' is the perfect ironic twist given the son-murdering scenario. Scores 8+ because the dark-comedy twist and character integration are genuinely exceptional.

jokes.text: And dental this time.
jokes.setup: Michael is listing demands: salary plus health benefits for three people; Wallace notes the cost is enormous
jokes.punchline: 'And dental this time' — Michael adds dental coverage as an afterthought to his already massive demands, the 'this time' implying the MSPC deliberately excluded dental
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum economy, great timing. 'This time' is the key phrase — it implies dental was previously unavailable at MSPC (of course it was, they're broke), and Michael adds it as a triumphant demand. The casual escalation of his demands to include dental — as if he's been denied dental his whole life and now he will have it — is very funny.

jokes.text: These are our demands. Your company cannot be worth that much. — Our company is worth nothing. That's the difference between you and I. Business isn't about money to me, David. If tomorrow my company goes under, I will just start another paper company. And then another and another and another. I have no shortage of company names. That's one of 'em!
jokes.setup: Wallace challenges Michael's demands by saying his company can't be worth that much
jokes.punchline: Michael agrees his company is worth nothing — then uses this as a philosophical point about business purity — then threatens an infinite sequence of paper companies — then reveals 'Another' is literally one of his company name ideas
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best moments. Michael's speech builds beautifully: (1) 'Our company is worth nothing' — true and said with pride; (2) 'Business isn't about money to me' — Michael's sincere anti-capitalist naivety; (3) the threat to start infinite paper companies reveals Michael as genuinely undeterrable; (4) 'I have no shortage of company names. That's one of 'em!' — the reveal that 'Another' is an actual company name in his repertoire is the perfect absurdist button. The joke scores high because each escalation lands, and 'That's one of 'em!' has the surprise-specific structure that makes it quotable and rewatchable. Michael's business philosophy accidentally becoming a negotiating superpower is peak character comedy.

jokes.text: This is a lot more than 60 grand. It's a multi-million dollar buyout.
jokes.setup: Michael's demands have escalated from $60,000 cash to jobs + salary + benefits + dental for three people
jokes.punchline: Wallace's dawning horror as he realizes MSPC has negotiated him from $60K to a multi-million dollar commitment is the joke — Michael has accidentally out-negotiated a CFO
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is situational — Wallace being out-negotiated by Michael is funny in context, and his shocked accounting of the escalated cost is the audience's reality check. Less a crafted joke than a plot-comedy moment.

jokes.text: Our balls are in your court.
jokes.setup: Michael closes his negotiating ultimatum with a borrowed sports expression
jokes.punchline: 'Our balls are in your court' — Michael scrambles 'the ball is in your court' into a plural, vaguely inappropriate version
jokes.explanation: Michael's malapropism of 'the ball is in your court' into 'our balls are in your court' is very quotable and very Michael — the accidental anatomical suggestion, combined with Michael's complete sincerity, is characteristic of his best moments. Not a sophisticated joke structurally, but maximum character expression in five words.

jokes.text: There are certain defining moments in a person's life. The day he is born. The day he grows hair. The day he starts a business. And the day he sells that business back to Dunder Mifflin.
jokes.setup: Michael delivers a philosophical talking-head about life's defining moments
jokes.punchline: 'The day he grows hair' — this is inserted between 'the day he is born' and 'the day he starts a business' as if it belongs there. Also the entire speech is about selling his company back to the company he left.
jokes.explanation: 'The day he grows hair' is the unexpected entry in an otherwise portentous list of milestones — it's a non-sequitur that suggests Michael equates puberty with business founding in terms of personal significance. The whole speech having 'the day he sells that business back to Dunder Mifflin' as its culminating event is also funny in context. Strong closing confessional.

jokes.text: What have I learned from all of this? It is far too early to tell. I am flying high and I don't even want to think about it. I just want to enjoy it.
jokes.setup: Michael's closing talking-head reflects on what he's taken away from the MSPC experience
jokes.punchline: 'It is far too early to tell' — Michael's self-reflection immediately bottoms out into admitting he has no idea what he's learned, and he doesn't want to think about it
jokes.explanation: A good closing joke — Michael's takeaway from a major life event is that it's 'too early to tell' what his takeaway is. The lack of any self-examination, dressed up in the language of self-examination, is perfectly Michael. It's also oddly relatable as a coda. Good closing beat.

jokes.text: You're done.
jokes.setup: Michael is in the middle of enjoying his victory in a talking-head
jokes.punchline: Someone (presumably a crew member or producer) flatly tells Michael 'You're done.' — cutting off his reverie. Michael had been mid-celebration.
jokes.explanation: A meta-joke ending — the crew dismissing Michael mid-celebration is a tiny deflation that works as a gentle punchline to the entire episode. Economy is near-perfect but it's a minor beat.

tmdb_overview: Michael's new company struggles to make early morning deliveries while the office tries to get their expense reports in on time after Angela enforces Dunder Mifflin's policy.
